---
pagetitle: The Software Engineer Reborn
---

## The Software Engineer Reborn

- A vision of human–AI collaboration.

::: {.notes}

Talk is partly an exploration of what’s happening to me, the role, and the world.
I’ve tried to anchor it in my experience but I couldn’t help pontificate a little.
Hopefully it is helpful regardless of what stage you are in your career as a software engineer, you learn some tricks about using AI, and it provokes some thought about the interaction of AI with society.
I don’t want it to be doom and gloom, don’t want to make light of the uncertainty, or to suggest that fear and anxiety are not present or warranted.
With that said, lots is happening right now… and I will note that death is a pre-requisite  of rebirth. :::

## AI is going to transform society

- I can take ideas much further than I could before.
- More people can create useful software.
- More kinds of work can become software.

::: {.notes}

The expansion of capability is why I take this seriously.

:::

## Huge possibilities. Consequential choices.

- What becomes possible?
- Who pays for the infrastructure and resource use?
- Who receives the benefits?
- What risks are we creating?

::: {.notes}

Brief context: optimism, misuse, environmental costs, and the distribution of gains.

:::

## The title can survive while the work changes

- The role: what we do, what employers need, what earns compensation.
- The person: what we enjoy, what we value, who we understand ourselves to be.

::: {.notes}

A sufficiently changed role can feel like a different profession.

:::

## How I arrived here

- Neuroscience → scientific software → infrastructure and backend → AI-assisted full-stack work.

::: {.notes}

Tell the personal trajectory through the changes in what I could do.

:::

## The boundaries of my work expanded

- Front ends.
  Infrastructure.
  Browser testing.
  Deployment.
- I can carry an idea much further toward a complete product.

::: {.notes}

Use one or two existing artifacts to make that expanded range visible.

:::

## What becomes worth attempting?

- A useful idea no longer has to justify months of learning a new stack.
- Smaller, more personal problems become worth solving.

::: {.notes}

The car-comparison dashboard is one possible example; choose the artifact I most want to discuss.

:::

## Why engineering was satisfying

- I could immerse myself in a difficult problem.
- The effort produced understanding.
- I could build a solution and explain why it worked.
- That expertise was useful and valued.

::: {.notes}

Establish what the old way of working gave me before describing what changed.

:::

## Expanded capability, lost mastery

- I can produce work across more domains.
- I retain less of its detail.
- Some of the pleasure of personally solving the problem is gone.

::: {.notes}

Talk about the change in satisfaction and the attempt to develop mastery of this new way of working.

:::

## Quality ≠ ownership

- The artifact may be better.
- It can still be harder to explain, defend, caveat, or fully stand behind.

::: {.notes}

This is a central tension in the new work.

:::

## The exhaustion is different

- More possibilities to explore.
- More unfamiliar work to assess.
- More decisions to make.
- A collaborator with no natural stopping point.

::: {.notes}

Connect cognitive saturation to the expansion of work, context, and responsibility.

:::

## What does an engineer contribute?

- Making: How can this be built?
- Directing: What should happen next?
- Deciding: Which outcomes and tradeoffs matter?
- Connecting: What will people understand, trust, and use?

::: {.notes}

These dispositions give us a way to examine the changing balance of our work.

:::

## What we bring with us

- Decomposing ambiguous problems.
- Working through abstractions.
- Testing assumptions against reality.
- Investigating failures.
- Making systems dependable.

::: {.notes}

Our experience supplies useful starting habits for the transition.

:::

## What we need to develop

- Understanding the domain and the people affected.
- Choosing worthwhile outcomes.
- Coordinating expertise.
- Communicating intent and uncertainty.

::: {.notes}

AI also lets domain experts approach implementation from the other direction.

:::

## Knowing what matters and making it work

- Outcome: Does this solve a worthwhile problem?
- System: Can it be operated, evaluated, maintained, and relied upon?

::: {.notes}

Engineers and domain experts increasingly need parts of each other’s expertise.

:::

## Two productive patterns

- The knowledge worker: use AI to produce a particular artifact.
- The systems engineer: build AI into a capability that performs a class of tasks repeatedly.

::: {.notes}

The distinction helps explain both the opportunities and the work of assessing quality.

:::

## Making an artifact easier to assess

- Preserve sources, assumptions, calculations, tests, and decisions.
- Make the important questions easy for an expert to investigate.

::: {.notes}

The work includes making the result assessable without independently reconstructing everything.

:::

## Engineering a scalable capability

- Define a sufficiently bounded task.
- Evaluate behavior across cases.
- Establish operating limits.
- Improve reliability and economics.

::: {.notes}

This is another direction for engineering: turning flexible intelligence into a usable, repeatable service.

:::

## The code has moved into the background

- In an IDE, code occupied the center of my attention.
- Now I work through projects, conversations, instructions, artifacts, and decisions.

::: {.notes}

Begin the workspace walkthrough here.
Show the environment as it exists.

:::

## The expanding set of threads I track

- Several projects.
- Several lines of work within a project.
- Explorations, alternatives, and implementation in parallel.
- Results returning for attention.

::: {.notes}

Show how work branches and how I move between it.

:::

## Compression becomes central

- What does the agent need to know?
- What do I need to understand?
- What must survive when we return to this work?

::: {.notes}

Show the role of project context, instructions, skills, and short records of decisions.

:::

## How I keep a relationship to the work

- Artifacts and version history.
- Milestones and review.
- Permissions and execution boundaries.
- Knowing what I am ready to accept.

::: {.notes}

Use the workspace to connect selective ownership with the practical choices I make.
End the walkthrough.

:::

## Would I choose this work again?

- Impact.
  Compensation.
  Enjoyment.
- Lifestyle.
  Community.
  Agency.

::: {.notes}

The disruption prompts a fresh look at the reasons for choosing this career; my priorities have also changed over time.

:::

## Different directions are opening

- A broader knowledge worker.
- Directing and refining AI-assisted production.
- Engineering bounded, scalable AI systems.
- Conventional development where security and direct control matter.

::: {.notes}

Which activities fit my strengths, interests, and preferred working life?

:::

## We still need other people

- Expertise beyond our own.
- People who can challenge and assess our work.
- Shared standards.
- Community and belonging.

::: {.notes}

Include the role of experienced and retired engineers in sharing judgment and helping people learn.

:::

## Starting over carries a cost

- The skills I have accumulated.
- The work I enjoy.
- The identity I have built.
- The future I had expected.

::: {.notes}

Allow room for grief and self-compassion alongside curiosity and excitement.

:::

## Act while there are choices to explore

- Try the new ways of working.
- Notice what is changing around you.
- Reassess what you want.
- Make room to change direction.

::: {.notes}

Close on agency: bend with the change rather than discovering belatedly that the reasons for choosing the work no longer hold.

:::
